Yeah, I'm here. What do you want to know?

During normal operations, nuclear power plants have an extremely low carbon footprint. Depending on the design, some of the plant's systems power source is the municipal grid or "town power", so it's not 100% carbon free.

But that's not the end of the story. Uranium doesn't grow on trees, it has to be mined, transported, refined, enriched (for non Candu reactors) and processed into fuel bundles. These steps are energy intensive processes that can release carbon into the atmosphere.

Once the fuel is spent, it is stored in large pools and cooled for several years, until it is cool enough to be put into specially constructed containers (the building of which is an energy intensive process and causes carbon emissions as well). The spent fuel containers are then stored in structures that need to be manned, monitored and maintained for a very long time and nobody has a better solution for this issue; although I've heard tales of digging deep shafts in the Canadian Shield and burying waste there. This is not what normally happens to spent fuel.

During normal operation of the plant, there is a certain amount of low level radioactive (or likely active) waste that needs to be disposed of, off site; which is an expensive and energy intensive process. More carbon emissions.

But wait, there's more! Then the plants will need to be refurbished over their lifetime. This is a very energy intensive process that creates a lot of low level and higher level waste

There are back up generators that run on diesel that need to be fired up from time to time and maintained.

There are diesel fire pumps that need to be fired up from time to time and maintained.

And finally there are decommissioning activities. This is a tough one to wrap your head around so I'll put it this way: Eventually, where there is a big nuclear power plant, there will be a "green field". Everything that is there radioactive or not, will have to be removed and, for all intents and purposes, the land must be left in such a manner that it could be safely used as a public park.

So, while there is definitely a lower carbon footprint than coal power, those who say that nuclear plants are 100% carbon emission free are not being 100% accurate and not taking into account the entire life cycle of the plant. Also, those saying that coal plants are 100% not radioactive are also being 100% wrong, look it up.

EDIT: Source: I work in the nuclear industry and support it as the best option we have until it can be replaced by solar and wind power. We're not there yet, for a variety of reasons, but we are moving closer to more sustainable power sources and I support governments funnelling money to corporations that are pursuing sustainable power sources, as long as their lessons are not made secret as "proprietary knowledge", which I don't believe ever happens.
